preamble: Laxing of the close front vowel [i] to the near-close near-front [ɪ]. Middle English short /i/ became the lax /ɪ/ of Modern English kit (fisch /fiʃ/ > fish /fɪʃ/); Roger Lass dates the laxing to the 17th century, other scholars earlier. In Ukrainian, Old East Slavic и [i] merged with ы [ɨ] as [ɪ] (бити > бити [ˈbɪte] 'to beat'). In Central Javanese, /i/ is pronounced [ɪ] in closed syllables (mari [mari] 'to recover' but wit [wɪt] 'seedling'). In Turkish, /i/ is lowered to [ɪ] in the final open syllable of a phrase (kedi [cʰe̞ˈd̟ɪ] 'cat').

examples.note: Short /u/ was laxed to /ʊ/ in parallel (pullen > pull).

examples.from: Old East Slavic бити /ˈbʲitʲi/ 'to beat' (11th century)

examples.note: Old и [i] merged with ы [ɨ] as и [ɪ], and the preceding consonant lost its palatalization; Ukrainian [i], written і, comes from other sources.
Compare mari [mari] 'to recover', with /i/ in an open syllable.
Western (Banyumasan) Javanese keeps [i] in this position ([g̊ət̪ih]) and Eastern Javanese has [ɛ] ([g̊ət̪ɛh]).

languageExamples.context: Final open syllable of a phrase

examples.note: Wikipedia: /i, y, u, e, œ/ are lowered to [ɪ, ʏ, ʊ, ɛ, œ] in the final open syllable of a phrase (Zimmer & Orgun) or word-finally (Göksel & Kerslake, as cited by Wikipedia).

Wiktionary gives both [iˈcʰi̞] and [iˈcʰɪ]. It does not apply the rule consistently: gemi 'ship' [ɟeˈmi] and sevgi 'love' [s̪e̞vˈɟi] keep [i], while deniz 'sea' [d̪e̞ˈn̪ɪz̪̥] has [ɪ] in a closed syllable.
